explanations.answer: No one can cancel or amend it
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul says, “Even a human covenant, once it is ratified, cannot be canceled or amended.” Once the ink is dry, it's locked in. That's more than I can say for my New Year's resolutions, which lasted till about lunch.

explanations.answer: Only its maker can amend it
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but Paul doesn't carve out an exception for the maker. He says a ratified covenant “cannot be canceled or amended.” Not by the other side, and he doesn't say by the one who made it either. Once it's ratified, it stands.

explanations.answer: Both sides can still cancel it
explanations.explanation: Paul says the opposite, friend. A human covenant, once ratified, “cannot be canceled or amended.” If both sides could just walk away, nobody would bother signing anything. I'd be handing out cookies on a handshake and getting nothing back!

Yes, baker! Paul says the Scripture doesn't say “and to seeds,” meaning many, but “and to your seed,” meaning One, “who is Christ.” He's reading the promise to Abraham one little word at a time. One word, singular, and it points to Christ.

Isaac was Abraham's son (Genesis 21:3), so I see why you picked him. But Paul names who the One is, and it isn't Isaac. He says the seed is Christ. Sometimes the closest name on the list is just the closest name on the list.

Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is a big name, friend, but Paul doesn't give him the title here. In verse 16 he says the promise was spoken to Abraham and to his seed, meaning One, “who is Christ.” Moses doesn't make the list this time.

Close, but this one's flipped. Paul says the law that came 430 years later “does not revoke the covenant previously established by God.” So the law shows up late and doesn't nullify the promise. Being the newcomer doesn't give it the power to cancel anything.

Right, baker. Paul says the law that came 430 years later “does not revoke the covenant previously established by God, so as to nullify the promise.” The law arrives late, but it doesn't wipe out what came first. That's like a guy showing up at my bakery a half hour after the order was placed and trying to cancel it.
Exactly, friend. Paul says, “God freely granted it to Abraham through a promise.” Freely means nobody paid for it. A gift is a gift, and nobody can put a price sticker on it.

Not quite, baker. Paul says God “freely granted” the inheritance to Abraham through a promise. A reward gets earned, and a free gift doesn't. He says if the inheritance depends on the law, then it no longer depends on a promise.

Paul rules that one out himself. He says, “if the inheritance depends on the law, then it no longer depends on a promise.” But God gave it to Abraham through a promise. So the law isn't the way it came.
Yes, baker. Paul says the law “was added because of transgressions.” Transgressions are the wrongs people do. He also says it was added until the seed arrives, which tells us it had a set time.

That's a nice thought, friend, but it's not what Paul says. He says the law “was added because of transgressions.” Nothing there about a prize for the faithful. I've handed out plenty of cookies for good behavior, but Paul isn't running that kind of bakery.

Paul doesn't say that. He says the law “was added because of transgressions,” and he adds that no law was given that could impart life. If the law could do that, righteousness would have come from the law. So perfecting people isn't his answer.

That's right, baker. Paul says the law “was added because of transgressions, until the arrival of the seed to whom the promise referred.” So the law has a limit on it, and the limit is the seed. Earlier in verse 16, Paul told us the seed is Christ.

This one's true, friend. Paul says the law was added “until the arrival of the seed to whom the promise referred.” The law has an endpoint in what he says. And he already told us who the seed is: Christ.
Paul says no to that one, baker. He asks, “Is the law, then, opposed to the promises of God?” and answers, “Certainly not!” The law and the promises aren't enemies. He doesn't set them up as rivals.
That's it, friend. Paul asks if the law is opposed to the promises of God, and his answer is, “Certainly not!” He doesn't leave any wiggle room. When Paul says certainly not, he means certainly NOT.
Yes, baker. Paul says the promise is given “by faith in Jesus Christ” to “those who believe.” It goes to people who believe. And every one of them gets the same promise.

Good word, but it's not the one Paul uses. He says the promise might be given “by faith in Jesus Christ” to those who believe. The promise comes to believers by faith. I had to double check my own recipe notes on this one!

Waiting is something I know plenty about, friend, but that's not Paul's word here. He says the promise is given “by faith in Jesus Christ” to “those who believe.” The ones who receive it are the ones who believe.

explanations.answer: So we might be justified by faith
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Paul says, “the law became our guardian to lead us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith.” The guardian points toward Christ. And faith is how we're justified.

explanations.answer: So we might keep the law perfectly
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that, friend. He says the law led us to Christ “that we might be justified by faith.” Nothing about keeping it perfectly. I'd be the first one in line for perfect, and my cookies still come out a little lopsided.

explanations.answer: So we might earn the inheritance
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. Paul says God “freely granted” the inheritance through a promise, so it's not something earned. The reason the law led us to Christ is “that we might be justified by faith.” Faith is the answer, not earning.
It's the other way around, baker. Paul says, “Now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian.” So the guardian's job came with an end date. And he says it right in verse 25.
Right, friend. Paul says, “Now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian.” He doesn't leave us still under the guardian. The one doing the leading handed us over to Christ.
Yes, baker. Paul says, “You are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus.” Notice he says all. Everybody comes in the same way, through faith in Christ Jesus.

That's not what Paul says, friend. He says, “You are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus.” The law was our guardian, but faith is how we become sons. Same thing I'd tell a cookie cutter: the tool isn't the cookie!

Not family line, baker. Paul says it's “through faith in Christ Jesus.” He talks about being Abraham's seed too, but he says that's because we belong to Christ (Galatians 3:29). Faith opens the door, not the family tree.

That's right, baker. Paul says, “For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ.” Clothed is the picture he uses. And I'm still working on getting my apron to stay clean past ten o'clock.

This one's true, friend. Paul says, “For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ.” That's the picture he gives. Everyone baptized into Christ, with no one left out.

Paul says the opposite, baker. He says, “There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” Three pairs, and not one of them stays in a separate group. All one.
Yes, friend. Paul says, “for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female are all one. That's a whole lot of folks fitting in a single batch!
Yes, baker. Paul says, “And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's seed.” Earlier he said the seed is One, who is Christ (Galatians 3:16). So belonging to Christ puts you in that family.
That's it, friend. Paul says you're “heirs according to the promise.” The promise is what the inheritance goes by. And God gave Abraham that inheritance freely (Galatians 3:18).

Not this one, baker. Paul says you're heirs “according to the promise,” not according to the law. He's already said the inheritance doesn't depend on the law. Law is a good word, but it doesn't fit either blank.
Close to the neighborhood, friend, but not the word. Paul says you are Abraham's “seed.” Servants isn't in the verse. Later he says you are no longer a slave, but a son (Galatians 4:7).

That's not in the verse, baker. Paul says you're heirs “according to the promise,” not according to works. He already told us God “freely granted” the inheritance through a promise (Galatians 3:18). No work gets stamped on this one.

explanations.answer: The date set by his father
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Paul says the heir “is subject to guardians and trustees until the date set by his father.” The father picks the date. The heir doesn't get to hurry it along, however many times he checks the calendar.
Paul doesn't say that, friend. He says the heir is under guardians and trustees “until the date set by his father.” Marriage doesn't come into it. The father sets the date.
Paul doesn't give an age, baker. He says the heir is under guardians and trustees “until the date set by his father.” No number shows up in the verse. It's his father's date.
Yes, baker. Paul says, “when the time had fully come, God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law.” God sent His own Son. And He sent Him when the time had fully come.

Angels show up earlier in this passage, friend. Paul says the law was administered through angels (Galatians 3:19). But in verse 4 he says, “God sent His Son.” That's who came when the time had fully come.

Paul doesn't say prophet, baker. He says, “God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law.” The Son is who God sent when the time had fully come. That's a different kind of delivery altogether.

explanations.answer: To redeem those under the law
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. Paul says God sent His Son “to redeem those under the law.” And the Son was “born under the law” Himself. He came to where they were.

explanations.answer: To add more to the law
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that, baker. He says the Son was sent “to redeem those under the law.” Redeem is the word he uses. He gives no hint of adding to the law.

explanations.answer: To judge those under the law
explanations.explanation: Not judge, friend. Paul says God sent His Son “to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons.” That's the purpose he gives, and it's a gift.

Yes, baker! Paul says God sent His Son “to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons.” Adoption as sons is the goal he names. I'll tell you, I know a little something about being picked up and brought home.

This one's true, friend. Paul says the Son was sent “to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons.” Adoption as sons is right there in verse 5. You can read it for yourself.
Yes, baker. Paul says the Spirit cries out, “Abba, Father!” That's what He calls God. Father, said from right inside our hearts.

Not master, friend. Paul says the Spirit of His Son cries out, “Abba, Father!” A master gives orders to a slave, and Paul says you're no longer a slave, but a son (Galatians 4:7). So the word is Father.
That's not the word, baker. Paul says the Spirit cries out, “Abba, Father!” The Spirit is sent into our hearts because we are sons. So the cry is a son's cry, and the word is Father.
That's it, baker. Paul says, “since you are a son, you are also an heir through God.” Son first, then heir. And Paul has been building toward this since the first verses of the passage.

Guests get a seat, friend, but Paul goes bigger. He says, “you are no longer a slave, but a son; and since you are a son, you are also an heir through God.” A guest doesn't inherit anything. A son does.
Not a worker, baker. Paul says, “you are no longer a slave, but a son.” He says since you are a son, you are “an heir through God.” Workers don't inherit the farm, but heirs do.
